As I started it and the characters are interesting, I've got no problem reading about awful people doing awful things and I liked how it delved into things like the KKK. 
Towards the end it went a bit weird, more thoughts in spoilers, but I wasn't satisfied with the end and it didn't feel like an end. I didn't understand what happened and it wasn't until reading someone else's review I even knew what had happened at the end, it was so vague. 
For me it would have been more impactful if it stayed smaller and more real, like I was way less emotionally invested towards the end of the book. 
I did like it though I have some mixed feelings, was still a good read and I'm glad I read it and I'd read more by the author, but I'm not sure if it recommended this book often.
<spoiler>When the book went form a handful of murders to a mass scale thing it started to lose me. Instead of being about the characters I've learnt about it's just names of people. Especially as it started being racist people who genuinely were not great people, turning into just random white people which dilutes the message for me. 
Also the ending being about the guy writing names, I didnt clock at all what it was until I'd read another review. I know there are hints with rise and such, but I thought this was a realistic book and was expecting a more realistic ending. I would have preferred it too, it felt a bit hand-wavey, I would have liked a deeper discussion about how racism affected everyone, dialog about is revenge OK and such. Instead it was like nobody was responsible really and nothing comes of it.
I liked the rest of the book, shame about the ending. </spoiler>

Title: The Nights Are Quiet in Tehran
Contributors: Dana Haqjoo (Narrator), Anoushka Rava (Narrator), Ruth Martin (Translator)
Review:
A really interesting read. I listened to the audiobook and the narration was really good.
I like learning about how everything affects each family member and each generation in a different way. 
Without spoilers (history isn't a spoiler though), it's definitely a different vibe over time in Iran and people raised in different times and circumstances have such different views, it is really well done. Especially with how they relate to family. 
As I was listening I couldn't easily go back to check things and it took me a bit sometimes to figure out when the point of view switched, but generally it wasn't too bad to follow when it changed.
I actually think the changes in views really adds to this story and one of the things that makes is so poignant is how life has changed over the years and from a variety of perspectives. 
I did enjoy it, but I found I liked it more as someone who wants to learn more about the history of Iran, rather than about the characters. I wasn't particularly invested in the story itself, I was interested in the history. 
I think it may be better enjoyed in print, as I think the writing is really good but I don't think I got the full effect by audio, I may have enjoyed this book more if I read it physically. 
That's why I said this is good but not great.

Title: Will Grayson, Will Grayson
Review:
I really enjoyed reading this book. The comparison of the two main characters who have very little in common besides their name is very well done.
It's one of my favourite John Green books and I would recommend it to those who like his style and young adult books in general.

Title: The Illustrated Mum
Review:
Re-reading this in preparation for Picture Imperfect, having forgotten a lot of the story. A good but sad tale of the life of kids without good parents in their lives.
Dolphin annoys me somewhat as a character, but she is young so I kind of get it. I wish we heard from Star a bit more as I found her much more interesting, as the one who had to step in as a a parent and saw the writing on the wall a bit more. 
A good story, it doesn't stand up to reading as an adult as much as some other Jacqueline Wilson books but it's not bad either. Hopefully Picture Imperfect will follow on well.

Title: Land Quest
Review:
Potentially my favourite book of the quest series, there's just something special about this one that I love. Doing a reread this is one of the ones I look forward to the most. 
It's a fun switch, following a Lander in the World instead of the other way around. It's done really well and despite it being mostly set in the World the fantasy elements are carefully brought in in clever ways which I really enjoyed. 
Great book, would definitely recommend.

Title: The Light of All That Falls
Moods: adventurous, challenging, dark, emotional, mysterious, tense
Review:
I loved this book, sad that there's no more to read now I'm done with the series.
Definitely the best of the three for me, I liked following the different characters and Caeden really grew on me as his parts were some of my least favourite in the early books but I was so invested in his character arc here. 
Ashalia continues to be amazing, no notes, I just love her. 
Wirr is great too, seeing him learn how to do politics throughout the book and what is legal vs right shows growth and he's great too. 
Davian doesn't grow as much but he ready had so much in the earlier books I'm not complaining. I just wanted to see his journey and follow along and I was constantly wanting to know what would happen. 
Read this book in a few long sessions as it is so hard to put down, but so long you can't binge it if you want. It definitely needed to be that long though, I wouldn't have wanted anything taken away from it. 
The series as a whole is a great one, I hope we get the companion novel that was missing from this book as I'd love to go back into this world again. 
There is a lot to take in with all the books, so I'm sure one day I'll do a full reread, may leave it a while though. Few extra spoiler thoughts below, but loved this book and the series - fingers crossed for maybe a movie deal some day? 
<spoiler>I'm so glad Davian didn't have to die, after the shapeshifting bit I was wondering if someone could do it and he did and I'm so happy for it. Caeden dying makes so much more sense thematic wise too. 
So wanted to note Wirr leading the battle and almost everyone dying was so hard to read, so few people made it, he's basically the only survivor and it showed so much courage from Wirr, wanted to shout out that bit. 
I wish we had more character stuff from Asha, the d'yoken bit was good but mostly just her training. She might be my favourite, though her arc seemed more from the other books. 
I did like how this book ended with the three of them together, just as the first book started. They've barely been together at all throughout the story and it's nice to have them back together again, it felt like a full circle and I love that kind of thing. </spoiler>

Title: The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo
Review:
This book was great to read, it was easy to read and I didn't want it put it down. I wanted to know all about Evelyn Hugo and her life story.
I didn't see it was tagged as LGBTQ but I was so happy as it's rare you get LGBTQ romances as much in popular books, especially for bisexuality which is often completely ignored, I was so happy to read it as there is so little representation of it. It so well done I assume the author is LGBTQ if not bi and checked and she is. Not surprising given how well the story was told. 
It is a sad tale, as a lot of LGBTQ stories historically have been, with people not being able to be themselves and add in Hollywood being problematic in itself it's no wonder how things turned out. I think it's important to read these kind of stories, as we can forget what the past was like. 
Without spoilers, I really enjoyed the ending and reason why Monique was the one to tell the story. 
More thoughts in spoilers, an amazing book.
<spoiler>I knew there was something we weren't being told and we were given hints but I was surprised finding out about Monique's father, a great twist where it all makes sense and you realise she was vague for that part earlier. Well executed. 
Also I like that she knew she was dying, I kind of figured, but also it goes with Monique's piece on assisted dying, showing that Evelyn did appreciate her work outside of the link with her father.
No more notes, just loved this book. </spoiler>
